column4: The section’s s-m-w “name” gloss says naming raises the named one’s mention; here houses are to be raised, the Lord’s name mentioned, and He glorified. This gathers 87:1 and 87:15 into one practice.

The section’s s-m-w gloss makes a name an elevation of its bearer, while its dh-k-r gloss joins remembrance to honor; here the good word ascends to God and righteous work is raised, specifying how speech and action acquire height.

The section’s dh-k-r dictionary gloss calls remembrance “highness and honor”; 94:4 says God raised the Prophet’s remembrance, making the section’s elevation audible as honor rather than physical height.
The section joins the Lord’s name to glorification; this verse says the beautiful names belong to God and that all in the heavens and earth glorify Him, joining the two acts named in 87:1 and 87:15.

The section contrasts the Lord’s true highness with a creature’s claim to be highest; Pharaoh’s “الأعلى” is precisely that usurped title, so the scene makes false elevation answerable to the One glorified in 87:1.

The section’s ʿ-l-w dictionary gloss says that rising in the land can mean transgressing and magnifying oneself; this is the verdict on the one who “طغى,” the corrupt earthly height that the divine name displaces.

The section’s d-n-w gloss makes “الدنيا” the low, lesser, or nearer thing; this verse repeats the precise choice in 87:16, “آثر الحياة الدنيا,” inside the same judgment scene as Pharaoh’s transgression.

The section sets choosing the low worldly life against the Hereafter; this neighbor completes 79:38 by making the Fire the transgressor’s refuge, matching 87:12’s great Fire as the consequence of that choice.

The section’s opposite poles are the low worldly preference and the Lord’s highness; this neighbor turns to the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains desire, completing the reversal begun at 79:37–39 and echoing 87:10.
The section says the Hereafter is better and more enduring than the low, near life; this neighbor completes 79:40’s restraint with the Garden as refuge, the enduring alternative to 79:39’s Fire.

The section’s tasbīḥ gloss includes “نور” (light), which it links lexically to 87:12’s Fire; this verse calls God the Light of the heavens and earth, giving that light-family a divine illuminating use rather than the punitive Fire.

The section says tasbīḥ is declaring God free of every evil and links the great-fire word’s k-b-r family to magnifying God; this command joins glorification to the Lord’s name and greatness in one phrase.

The section links “سَبِّح” to declaring God above every evil and identifies k-b-r with magnifying Him; this verse explicitly commands glorification by the name of the Great Lord, matching 87:1’s name-and-praise.
The section’s tasbīḥ gloss supplies the act and its k-b-r gloss the divine magnification; this same command to glorify the great Lord names both, though it does not add the word “name” found in 87:1.
The section treats the Lord’s “name” as a bearer of elevated mention; this command to read by the name of the Lord who created connects that name to the Creator praised at the opening of 87.
The section joins the Lord’s name with remembrance and prayer; this command to remember the Lord’s name and devote oneself to Him gives that pairing a night-worship setting.
The section’s name-and-remembrance pairing is repeated here as a command to remember the Lord’s name morning and evening, extending the act across the day.
The section defines al-ʿulūw as height and explicitly turns to “the highest heavens”; this verse calls the heavens “العلى” and identifies their Creator as the source of the revelation.

The section’s ʿ-l-w root points to true height while warning that a ruler can corrupt it by self-exaltation; this verse declares God “تعالى,” the true King, locating sovereignty in God rather than a claimant such as Pharaoh.
The section makes “الأعلى” the high pole of its axis; in the Moses–Pharaoh contest God tells Moses, “أنت الأعلى,” turning the title away from Pharaoh’s claim and toward God’s supported messenger.

The section contrasts false self-exaltation with God-given elevation; after the magicians believe, this verse grants them “الدرجات العلى,” so genuine height is a reward for faith and righteous work, unlike Pharaoh’s claim in 79:24.

The section calls the Hereafter better and more enduring than the low life; this neighbor completes the high degrees of 20:75 with lasting Gardens and the reward of one who purifies himself, echoing 87:14 and 87:17.
The section evokes a shape rising into view; this preceding verse describes the figure as mighty and upright, while 53:7 supplies the highest horizon that completes the silhouette scene.

The section’s s-m-w dictionary branch describes a figure rising above the horizon until it can be made out; this verse places the figure at “الأفق الأعلى,” giving that horizon-and-height image a Quranic scene.
The section’s s-m-w branch evokes a shape emerging at the horizon and becoming visible; here the seen figure is “بالأفق المبين,” a direct horizon scene that clarifies the branch’s visual sense.

The section’s s-m-w dictionary branch calls the crescent’s visible form “سماوة الهلال” when it rises a little above the horizon; this verse asks about the new moons and identifies them as visible time-markers.

The section’s s-m-w branch specifically evokes the crescent rising above the horizon; this verse follows the moon’s phases until it returns like an old date-stalk, giving the crescent a concrete place in its cycle.
The section explicitly cites this aim: seeking the face of the “الأعلى” Lord. Its ʿ-l-w axis therefore distinguishes the giver’s devotion to God from a worldly claim to be highest.
The section pairs purification with remembrance and prayer; this neighbor identifies the person who gives his wealth in order to purify himself, the concrete act behind the aim at 92:20 and 87:14.

The section opposes the low, near worldly preference to devotion to the highest Lord; this neighbor says the giver seeks no repayment for a favor, clarifying that the giving at 92:18 is not a worldly exchange.
The section says the Hereafter is better and more enduring; this neighbor completes the giving and God-directed aim of 92:18–20 with the promised satisfaction.

The section contrasts those who turn from reminder and face the great Fire with the one who purifies and remembers; this verse says the most God-fearing will be kept from that Fire, the reverse fate in the same moral image.
The section’s 87:11–15 sequence sets the one who avoids reminder and burns in the great Fire against the one who purifies and remembers; this verse opens a parallel warning with the blazing Fire.
The section names the “أشقى” who burns in 87:12; this neighbor specifies that none but the most wretched will burn in the Fire introduced at 92:14.

The section contrasts the person who fears and remembers with one who avoids the reminder; this neighbor identifies the one who denies and turns away as the one who burns in the paired scene of 92:14–15.

The section connects remembrance of the Lord’s name to choosing the low worldly life; this verse sets turning away from remembrance beside desiring only the life of this world, making the choice a rejection of remembrance.

The section’s d-n-w gloss makes the worldly life the low or near choice, set against the better Hereafter; this verse describes people who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter and bar others from God’s way.
The section frames “الدنيا” as the lower choice against what endures; this verse says they preferred the life of this world over the Hereafter, giving that preference its explicit comparative form.

The section says the name “الدنيا” can carry nearness and lesser worth; this rebuke asks whether people are content with the worldly life in place of the Hereafter and calls its enjoyment small by comparison.
The section’s d-n-w gloss includes what is nearest; this verse names the immediate life (“العاجلة”) as what people love, sharpening the temporal-nearness side of its low-life image.
The section opposes the near life to the better, lasting Hereafter; this neighbor completes 75:20 by saying they leave the Hereafter, making the preference explicit.

The section’s d-n-w gloss includes the nearest or first thing; this verse calls worldly desire “العاجلة” and contrasts its quickly bounded provision with the Hereafter, where the section locates what lasts.
The section sets the low, near life against a better and enduring Hereafter; this neighbor completes 17:18 with the one who seeks the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer.

The section calls the worldly life the low or near pole and says the Hereafter is better and more lasting; this verse directly contrasts worldly enjoyment and adornment with what is better and more enduring with God.

The section distinguishes the low life from what endures; this neighbor completes 28:60 by asking whether one promised a good promise to meet it is like one given worldly enjoyment and then brought to judgment.

The section says the low, near worldly life is outweighed by the better and more enduring Hereafter; this verse uses that same comparison and specifies that what is with God is better and more lasting.
The section opposes the low worldly life to the lasting Hereafter; this verse calls the worldly life a temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the enduring home.
The section says the worldly life is low and the Hereafter better and lasting; this verse draws that boundary by calling this life play and amusement and the Hereafter the real life.
The section’s “الدنيا” is the lesser, near life; this verse contrasts the worldly life’s play and amusement with the Hereafter, which it calls better for the God-conscious.
The section’s low/near worldly pole is measured against what endures; this verse calls worldly life a deceptive enjoyment and locates success in being saved from the Fire and admitted to the Garden.
The section presents the worldly life as a preferred, lesser good; this verse names the attractions that beautify it, calls them worldly enjoyment, and contrasts them with the good return with God.

The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss warns that earthly rising can mean arrogant self-exaltation; this verse reserves the Hereafter for those who do not desire “علوا في الأرض” or corruption, the direct boundary to Pharaoh’s claim.

The section warns that al-ʿulūw can be corrupted into self-exaltation; this verse forbids walking arrogantly and sets the body’s limits against earth and mountains, a concrete boundary on human height.

The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss describes a ruler rising in the land by tyrannizing and magnifying himself; Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest is paired here with his attempt to build a tower reaching toward the heavens.
The section’s highness axis exposes the ruler who magnifies himself; this neighbor says Pharaoh and his forces were arrogant in the land, completing the tower scene of 28:38.
The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss makes a ruler’s self-raised status corrupt; here Pharaoh orders a tower so he might reach the routes to the heavens, turning claimed supremacy into a literal, futile ascent.
The section contrasts true divine height with a ruler’s claim; this neighbor completes Pharaoh’s tower order by showing its failure and his delusion about Moses’ God.
The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss defines earthly rising as transgression and self-magnification; this verse names Qarun, Pharaoh, and Haman as arrogant in the land despite Moses’ clear proofs.

The section’s k-b-r gloss distinguishes true greatness from self-claimed grandeur; this verse depicts a person turning away and “استكبر,” a concrete form of false elevation before he rejects the reminder.

The section says ʿ-l-w can mean transgressing and magnifying oneself; this verse says the human being transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient, locating false height in imagined independence.
The section exposes self-exalting height as corrupt; this neighbor completes 96:6 by stating the trigger for that transgression, the person’s sense that he has no need.

The section’s 87:12–13 describes the Fire as a punishment in which one neither dies nor lives; this verse gives that same suspended state for the criminal in Hell, and 20:75 supplies the contrasting high degrees of the believers.

The section cites the powerful figure standing before the highest horizon in 53:7; this preceding verse describes the figure as mighty and upright, while 53:7 supplies the horizon that completes the silhouette scene.

The section’s horizon image can be read as a figure seen at a distance; after 53:7 places him at the highest horizon, this verse says he drew near and descended, changing distance within the same scene.
The section’s s-m-w branch is about a rising figure made visible; this neighbor measures the approach described in 53:8 as two bow-lengths or nearer, adding scale to the horizon scene.
The section connects the horizon figure with revelation; this neighbor completes the approach of 53:8–9 by saying revelation came to His servant.

The section’s dh-k-r dictionary gloss includes honor and high mention, while the surah also centers reminder; this verse calls the message a reminder, showing the related but distinct admonitory sense.
The section links remembrance to honor; this neighbor specifies that whoever wills may remember the reminder introduced in 80:11, rather than treating the word as only public renown.
The section’s remembrance-and-elevation image has a textual counterpart in this continuation: the reminder is in honored pages, giving the act of remembering a dignified setting.
The section’s s-m-w imagery is elevation and its dh-k-r gloss is honor; this neighbor calls those pages “مرفوعة مطهرة,” joining elevation to purity.

The section’s elevation and honor image continues here: 80:15 places the pages in the hands of scribes, and this verse calls their bearers noble and dutiful, specifying the honored setting introduced in 80:13.

The section’s al-ʿulūw image treats highness as a bestowed rank; this verse says God raises those who believe and those given knowledge by degrees, clarifying that genuine rank is granted, not seized.
The section’s al-ʿulūw axis belongs to the Lord; this verse closes by naming God “العلي العظيم,” coupling divine highness and greatness rather than a ruler’s self-claim.
The section joins al-ʿulūw and k-b-r, distinguishing God’s greatness from false self-exaltation; this verse calls God “العلي الكبير,” a direct divine pairing of the two axes.
The section’s height and greatness axis points to God as its true bearer; this verse likewise says “العلي الكبير,” anchoring those qualities in divine truth and sovereignty.
The section’s al-ʿulūw and k-b-r roots make highness and greatness divine qualities; this verse names God “العلي الكبير” after fear leaves the hearts, joining divine greatness with reverence.
The section’s axis assigns true height to God; this verse calls Him “العلي العظيم,” a direct divine height-and-greatness formula.
The section’s ʿ-l-w family includes exaltation and height; this verse calls God “المتعال” while describing His knowledge of unseen and seen, locating transcendence in the knower.

The section contrasts God’s true greatness with human self-magnification; this verse says greatness in the heavens and earth belongs to God, placing the grandeur claimed by rulers under divine ownership.

The section’s k-b-r dictionary gloss gives greatness and also permits self-inflated grandeur; this verse names God “المتكبر” and immediately glorifies Him above partners, separating divine majesty from a creature’s claim.
The section makes tasbīḥ the act of declaring God free of every evil; this verse opens with everything in the heavens and earth glorifying Him, extending the named act to the whole created scene.
The section’s s-b-ḥ gloss defines glorification as declaring God pure; this verse says the heavens, earth, and all within them glorify Him, giving the command a cosmic scope.

The section’s ʿ-l-w dictionary branch says “تعال” originally calls someone to a high place; here the call is “تعالوا إلى كلمة سواء,” shifting that upward invitation into a summons to a shared word about worshiping God alone.

The section’s s-m-w branch evokes the crescent becoming visible as it rises above the horizon; this verse stages the moon following the sun, a specific paired movement across the sky that frames that rising image.

The section’s whole surah says of the condemned that they neither die nor live, while its tasbīḥ gloss exalts God; this verse commands glorification of the Ever-Living who does not die, a precise boundary between divine life and the Fire’s suspended state.

The section defines tasbīḥ as declaring God free of every evil and sets true divine highness against self-claimed grandeur; this verse glorifies and exalts God far above what they say, including their claim of great elevation.
The section’s tasbīḥ gloss is God’s purification from every evil; this closing command glorifies the Lord of might above what they attribute, locating true majesty in God.
The section says the name identifies its bearer and raises the named one’s mention; this verse assigns the most beautiful names to God and commands calling on Him by them.
The section joins the Lord’s name to exaltation and honor; this verse blesses the name of the Lord who possesses majesty and honor, making the name itself the site of that reverence.
The section places the Lord’s name at the center of glorification; this verse permits calling God or the Most Merciful and says the most beautiful names belong to Him.
The section’s first image glorifies the Lord’s name; this verse identifies God as the sole deity and says the most beautiful names are His, specifying the bearer of the names.

The section’s k-b-r gloss includes magnifying God with the takbīr; this command praises God as having no child or partner and calls for magnifying Him greatly, directing grandeur to its proper bearer.
The section ties al-aʿlā to the Creator; this verse says God originates and repeats creation and that the highest attribute belongs to Him in the heavens and earth.

The section’s d-n-w gloss includes what is low or lesser, and its central choice is the lower life over the better Hereafter; this verse uses “أدنى” for the inferior thing chosen in place of what is better, a concrete but worldly-food instance of that lower-for-better exchange.

The section contrasts the high with the low or near; this verse calls the nearest heaven “السماء الدنيا,” giving that low/near pole a literal place in the sky and contrasting it with the section’s highest heavens.
The section’s d-n-w gloss includes the nearer thing and its ʿ-l-w axis the highest; this verse names the nearest heaven and describes its adornment, making the same vertical scale cosmic.
The section’s low/near and high poles can describe the sky as well as worldly life; this verse specifically calls the adorned heaven the nearest one, a spatial use of “الدنيا.”

The section’s d-n-w dictionary gloss includes what is nearest; this verse locates the Romans’ defeat in the nearest land, preserving that spatial sense of the root apart from the moral choice of worldly life.

The section’s s-m-w dictionary branch evokes the crescent becoming visible above the horizon; this verse says the moon has measured phases, giving the crescent a place in the recurring lunar cycle and its timekeeping use.

The section’s s-m-w branch names the crescent rising above the horizon; this verse swears by the moon when full, a later visible phase that completes the crescent’s growth rather than repeating the crescent itself.
The section warns that highness can become self-exaltation; this verse says Iblis was arrogant and among the disbelievers, identifying the refusal behind a false claim to rank.

The section distinguishes granted divine highness from self-claimed grandeur; God asks Iblis whether he was arrogant or among the exalted, making the claim to rank the issue of the command to prostrate.
The section’s axis exposes self-awarded superiority; this neighbor gives Iblis’s reason for refusing, his claim that he is better because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay.
The section links corrupted height to arrogance; Iblis answers the command to prostrate by claiming he is better than Adam, a direct self-ranking rather than bestowed elevation.
The section warns that ʿ-l-w can turn into self-exaltation; God rebukes Iblis’s arrogance and orders him to descend, making the high/low reversal explicit.

The section’s k-b-r family distinguishes divine greatness from a creature’s self-importance; this verse says Iblis refused and grew arrogant, the original scene of a creature resisting God’s command through claimed rank.

The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss says a ruler’s rising in the land can mean tyranny and self-magnification; this verse says Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people, giving that corruption its political scene.

The section connects false highness with Pharaoh; after Moses and Aaron bring clear signs, this verse says Pharaoh and his chiefs were arrogant, a repeated account of resistance to divinely backed truth.
The section’s image opposes true highness to a ruler’s self-claimed supremacy; Pharaoh boasts of his kingdom and the rivers beneath him, grounding his status claim in worldly dominion.
The section presents Pharaoh as claiming the highest place; this neighbor completes his boast by belittling Moses as insignificant and barely able to make himself clear.

The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss warns of arrogant rising on earth; this verse says God turns away from His signs those who act arrogantly in the land, a direct boundary between self-exaltation and receiving guidance.

The section contrasts a ruler’s earthly self-exaltation with genuine elevation; this verse says heaven’s gates will not open to those who deny God’s signs and act arrogantly, setting a boundary on their claimed ascent.
The section makes al-aʿlā the image of elevation; this verse says God raised Idris to a high station, showing rank as something bestowed rather than claimed.

The section contrasts Pharaoh’s claimed highness with true rank; this verse says God made people successors and raised some above others in degrees as a test, presenting elevation as assigned and accountable.

The section says the near worldly life is surpassed by what is better and more enduring; this verse calls wealth and children adornments of worldly life, but says enduring good deeds are better with the Lord for reward and hope.

The section says the Hereafter is better and more enduring than the low worldly life; this verse contrasts what people possess and what is with God, saying the former ends while what is with God remains.

The section defines worldly life as low and near against the Hereafter; this verse directs people to seek the Hereafter with what God has given them while not forgetting their share of this world, qualifying how the lower life may be used.
The section says the worldly life is the lower choice beside what lasts; this verse describes people rejoicing in worldly life and calls its enjoyment small compared with the Hereafter.
The section names the choice of the low worldly life; this verse describes those who desire the present life and its adornment, connecting that preference to deeds done for its reward.
The section says the Hereafter is better and more enduring than worldly life; this neighbor completes 11:15 by saying what its seekers gain there and that they have no share in the Hereafter.

The section contrasts remembrance of the Lord with preferring the low worldly life; this verse warns against following someone whose heart is heedless of remembrance and who follows desire, a specific opposite stance to the one who fears and remembers.
The section links remembrance of the Lord’s name with prayer and glorification; this command to believers to remember God much repeats the remembrance side of that pairing.
The section joins remembrance to glorifying the Lord; this neighbor completes 33:41 by commanding glorification morning and evening, giving the paired acts a daily rhythm.

The section places God’s true highness above a creature’s self-claim; this verse rebukes people for failing to appraise God properly and depicts the earth held in His grasp and the heavens folded, setting divine scale beyond human grandeur.
The section’s tasbīḥ gloss is to declare God free of every evil; this verse denies God a child or partner and declares Him above what they describe, making that purification specific.
The section defines tasbīḥ as declaring God above every evil; this verse announces God’s command and glorifies Him above what they associate with Him, a direct instance of that act.

The section assigns true highness to God and exposes self-claimed grandeur; this verse says the highest description belongs to God, setting divine measure against the deficient example it attributes to those who deny the Hereafter.
